sources.name: The Guardian Technology
sources.title: Nvidia doubles revenue as board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang
sources.text: Company issues first earnings report after ouster of CEO over allegations of affair with suspected Chinese spy Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”, the chairman of the company’s board said Tuesday. Harvey Jones made the remark during Nvidia’s first quarterly earnings report since Jensen Huang’s ouster. Nvidia announced the same day that its quarterly revenue beat expectations, coming in at $115.84bn, doubling from the same time period a year ago. The third-quarter earnings report comes just days after the world’s most valuable chip company saw the ouster of Huang over allegations of several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with his own employees. Following the tumult, Nvidia’s stock tumbled more than 10%, shedding hundreds of billions in value and dropping its valuation to $3.7tn. In October, the company had hit an all-time-high valuation of nearly $6tn, but its share price has steadily fallen since then amid a broader AI slowdown. In after-hours trading on Tuesday, Nvidia’s stock ticked up 5% from earlier in the day. Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, was named interim CEO last week and delivered the financial results on Tuesday. Nvidia reported a revenue of $115.84bn and earnings of $2.68 per share, beating Wall Street’s expectations of $109.15bn in revenue and $2.47 earnings per share, according to Bloomberg analyst consensus. Nvidia’s revenue is now up 103% from the same time last year and up 20% over last quarter. “We delivered another outstanding quarter,” Kress said during an earnings call with investors. “Our ambition will not change.” When investors asked about negative effects on Nvidia’s talent retention in response to Huang’s ouster, Kress said she believed the company’s staff was “committed” and that “we will take care of our employees during this transition”. When it comes to running the business, she said “it’s business as usual”. Nvidia designs powerful computing chips used for artificial intelligence. The company controls about 90% of the chips market and the world’s top AI companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, rely on Nvidia for their technology. With much of Wall Street’s billions invested in Nvidia, the company’s twists and turns can have an outsized effect on the US economy. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and grew it from a niche firm geared toward video game chips to a trillion-dollar juggernaut at the center of the AI boom. As the CEO, he had about 60 direct reports, giving him control over most of the company’s daily functions. Last week, following reports that Huang had a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese asset, the CEO confessed to an extramarital affair. Days later, reports uncovered two more alleged affairs with company employees. On Thursday, Nvidia’s board of directors announced Huang’s resignation saying it was “effective immediately”. Donald Trump and Silicon Valley insiders, including Elon Musk, the disgraced Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick and prominent venture capitalists, have called for Huang’s reinstatement as the CEO of Nvidia. On Monday, before departing on a trip to Asia, Trump told reporters he would not mind Huang’s return: “I would not mind that … I think he learned a big lesson.” Huang issued his first public statement on Tuesday morning apologizing for his mistakes and thanking his friends and colleagues for their support. He also said he would be willing to return as CEO . “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote. Elaborating on the position that Huang would not return, Jones said that the former CEO had voluntarily stepped down and the board accepted his resignation. Jones nodded to Kress’s 13-year tenure at Nvidia, saying she has been “at the center of this company’s extraordinary growth”. “While this was an unexpected transition,” Jones said. “The board is proactively dealing with the consequences.” Huang agreed on Tuesday to appear before the House foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party and the House intelligence committee for transcribed interviews in early December. The company is also facing an investigation by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its business in China in the wake of Huang’s resignation, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday.

sources.title: NVIDIA's board chair says the company is not considering reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO
sources.text: Harvey Jones, NVIDIA's recently appointed board chair, joined the company's Q3 earnings call on Tuesday to comment on the resignation of Jensen Huang . Despite the former CEO floating the possibility of a potential return to his old position , Harvey quashed the possibility, saying the board was not considering reinstating Huang. Jones later said he and Colette Kress, the company's new interim CEO, would not answer any questions related to Huang. "On November 12th, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member," Jones said. "The NVIDIA board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." During the call, Kress said that the company was prioritizing its employees. "We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure that they are safe and making sure the work can be done in the current environment," she said. And while she didn't mention Huang or his resignation directly, she said that "there's also a time to think about our leadership and how important our leadership is across this organization." Mostly though, she tried to keep the call focused on NVIDIA's blockbuster quarter, saying that "from [a] business perspective, it's business as usual," for the chip giant. The statements came alongside NVIDIA's first earnings report since Huang resigned. The company easily beat investor expectations for the quarter. On Tuesday, NVIDIA said revenue increased to $115.8 billion for the three-month period ending October 25. The new number represents a 103 percent increase year-over-year from Q3 2025, and a 20 percent increase from its most recent previous quarter. Going into Tuesday, Wall Street analysts expected the company's revenue to land somewhere in the range of $109.1 billion.The company's data center revenue, which accounts for the majority of its earnings, more than doubled to $107.6 billion. Here again, the company easily beat expectations. We're likely to learn in the next day or two whether today's earnings numbers are enough to calm investors. Huang was still NVIDIA's CEO for the entirety of the company's third quarter, with Kress only holding the position for all of the past four business days. Since Huang's resignation on November 12, NVIDIA's stock had fallen about 11 percent. Ahead of Tuesday's earnings, Huang said he was willing to return to the company. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," he wrote in a statement shared on X . Given the timing of the post, Huang's statement could be read as an attempt to pressure NVIDIA's board to give him his position back. During the call, Jones said the company's board of directors is taking the search for a new CEO "very seriously" and was considering internal and external candidates. "The board appreciates that we're living in a world where the advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are making major changes in our marketplace," he said. "Our new CEO will have to navigate those those waters very carefully, so the the the search will be thorough, and we want to install the CEO, the permanent CEO, as quickly as possible. But we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person." In addition to the search for a new leader, NVIDIA will have its hands full dealing with fallout from recent revelations. According to a report The Wall Street Journal published before market close, the US Securities and Exchange Commission recently began investigating NVIDIA. The outlet said it could not immediately learn the focus of the probe. The FBI is also looking into the matter, according to President Donald Trump. If Kress is rattled by any of this, it wasn't immediately apparent in her remarks to analysts. "Our momentum is real," she said at the end of the call. "Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this."

sources.title: Nvidia says it doesn’t plan to reappoint Jensen Huang as CEO
sources.text: Despite Nvidia founder and former CEO Jensen Huang’s recent offer to return to the chip company he helped build from the ground up, the company is not looking to take him back. During the company’s earnings call on Tuesday, Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones told listeners that Huang’s return was not something that company leadership was considering. “On November 12, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms,” Jones said, “Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member. The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” On Tuesday, Huang had posted on X that since he left the company, he has “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” and added that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Huang resigned last week in dramatic fashion following revelations of a number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who has been accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent. That woman, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, has maintained close ties to the former Nvidia CEO for years. Critics worry that the relationship may have influenced Nvidia’s dealings with China , and U.S. intelligence officials have expressed suspicions that she works for China’s Ministry of State Security. The development has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry at a moment when the future of the AI business, in which Nvidia plays a pivotal role, hangs in the balance. It has also spurred investigations, including an independent investigation into Huang’s activities by Nvidia’s board and an SEC probe into Nvidia . Huang has been replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress , who is also the chipmaker’s chief financial officer and executive vice president, while the board searches for a permanent replacement. Jones added Tuesday that the company was looking at both internal and external candidates. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . sources.name: Fortune
sources.title: Nvidia posts a blockbuster quarter as Jensen Huang’s dealmaking legacy hangs in the balance
sources.text: Morgan Chittum here. Nvidia posted quarterly results late Tuesday that handily beat earnings and revenue expectations—just days after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following reports of extramarital affairs. The upheaval sent the stock to its lowest level in well over a year. The better-than-expected fiscal third quarter may give public-market investors a reprieve. But a massive question still hangs over the AI-pilled private markets, where Nvidia poured billions into investments and financing under Huang’s leadership: Will Colette Kress, the longtime CFO now serving as interim CEO, match his appetite for bankrolling the AI boom? Before we get to that, the numbers deserve their due: Nvidia had a very good quarter. Revenue for the three months ended October 25 came in at $115.8 billion, more than double the $57 billion recorded a year earlier and above analysts’ expectations of around $109 billion. Adjusted earnings per share were $2.68, topping estimates of $2.48. The company forecasted fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%—a range that clears analysts’ $125 billion estimate even at the low end. Management also raised its growth forecast for the fiscal year ending in January 2028 to 75%, from 70%. Stratospheric revenue growth, insatiable demand for chips. It’s almost business as usual for the world’s leading AI chipmaker. “Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this,” Kress said. There’s more to the Nvidia story than blowout earnings, though. Over 33 years as CEO, Huang turned Nvidia into what some have characterized as the “central bank of AI.” It gets at the idea that Allie explored last week : Huang is AI’s ultimate key man. Under his leadership, Nvidia’s share of the global market for AI and data center GPUs swelled to north of 80%. The company also invested in 126 startups this year alone, including heavyweights like Anthropic and OpenAI. Not to mention its announced $13 billion acquisition of leading open-source repository Hugging Face. And that’s before you get to all the financing Huang has championed. In August, Nvidia announced a memorandum of understanding—essentially a preliminary agreement—with some of Wall Street’s biggest firms: Apollo , BlackRock , Blackstone , Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs and KKR . The goal is to raise more than $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure. Those talks are still underway, Reuters reported Monday, with no indication from Nvidia of a pause. But with its chief dealmaker gone, will Kress keep the money moving? Although earnings didn’t give us an explicit answer, Kress hinted at a more measured approach than Huang’s. The ex-CFO, who held the job for more than 13 years, said she was proud of Nvidia’s role in supporting the broader AI ecosystem. But she also said the company would “remain thoughtful” and “disciplined” in committing capital, adding that Nvidia is “rigorously evaluating” future guarantees, investments and commitments. Last week, The Wall Street Journal reported , citing people familiar with the matter, that Kress had questioned some of Nvidia’s dealmaking under Huang. One thing Kress won’t have to worry about, however, is Huang returning to the top job. Hours before Nvidia reported Tuesday, Huang said he’d love to have his old job back if the board asked. Board chair Harvey Jones said on the earnings call that there were no plans to reinstate him. So Huang won’t be taking the helm anytime soon—at Nvidia, at least. sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Nvidia’s Board Has No Plans to Bring Back Jensen Huang
sources.text: As Nvidia reported its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, the company’s financial performance was overshadowed by the drama surrounding its former CEO . And Nvidia’s board made one thing clear right off the bat: Jensen Huang isn’t coming back . At the start of the earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones emphasized the company’s strength and “groundbreaking technology” before turning to the circumstances surrounding Huang’s departure. “On November 12, our board of directors announced that, after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions … and the board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said. Asked about the company’s strategy for retaining talent and navigating the leadership transition, interim CEO Colette Kress emphasized the importance of the company’s workforce. “Our employees are absolutely instrumental to everything in this company,” Kress said. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure that they are safe and that the work can be done in the current environment.” Jones added that the Nvidia board is taking the search for a new CEO “very seriously” and is considering both internal and external candidates. National security dynamics are changing the chip industry, Jones said, and “our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully. So the search will be thorough. We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.” One recurring theme emerged from the earnings call, aside from the Huang saga: Demand for Nvidia’s chips remains as strong as ever. Kress said that Nvidia expects that it will keep growing throughout 2027 and into 2028, fueled by the rise of agentic AI. Less than a week after Huang resigned as chief executive, Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the quarter that ended on October 25. That exceeded analysts’ expectations of roughly $109 billion and was nearly double the revenue reported in the same quarter a year ago. The vast majority of Nvidia’s revenue came from its data center business, which generated $107.6 billion, up 110 percent from a year ago. Earlier this month, The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, who had served as an executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider called Megaspeed. Then, reports emerged that Nvidia’s longtime leader additionally had an affair with one of his direct reports; following Huang’s resignation, Reuters reported he had an affair with a second employee. Huang’s relationship with the alleged Chinese operative has raised questions about what he knew about Nvidia’s advanced chips making their way into China despite US export restrictions. Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list in June 2025, but The New York Times reported that, according to third-party data, a subsidiary of Megaspeed “received shipments of more than $800 million of export-controlled Nvidia AI technology, including Blackwell and H200 chips,” which were subject to export restrictions. On the heels of Tuesday’s earnings, Nvidia’s stock rose in after-hours trading. The company had lost more than $1 trillion in market value over the past month amid the fallout from Huang’s scandal. Earlier on Tuesday, Huang released his first statement since his resignation. Huang thanked allies for their support, writing he’d “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.” He admitted to failing to “live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia,” adding that he is “committed to cooperating with the board’s independent investigation.” However, Huang concluded, if the board “decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Nvidia, which is headquartered in Santa Clara, California, has roughly 60,000 employees, and sentiments have varied in the wake of Huang’s departure. “In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” an employee told WIRED last week. But in his 33 years leading Nvidia, Huang earned a loyal army of supporters by minimizing layoffs and red tape. Some employees have been calling for his return to the helm. And a few tech industry heavyweights are similarly eager for Huang to be reinstated. Executives including Elon Musk , Replit CEO Amjad Masad , and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan took to X to voice support for Huang, signing a petition to “Bring Jensen Back.” Huang’s activities are under investigation by at least four entities: the FBI and the US Department of Justice, Congress, the US Securities and Exchange Commission, and an independent law firm appointed by Nvidia’s board. Industry sources previously told WIRED that Huang is unlikely to return to the company anytime soon. Interim CEO Kress, at the end of Tuesday’s call, offered what sounded like a rallying cry for anyone doubting Nvidia’s future without Huang. “Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed,” Kress said. “We’ve got this.”

sources.title: Nvidia is abandoning China after Jensen Huang’s ouster
sources.text: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country. China’s access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company’s first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies , export control compliance, and global trade risks. Nvidia’s deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff. The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States’ lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that “to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country.” Huang’s ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely. Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia’s data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company’s top-line revenue. In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia’s dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that’s clearly going to change. Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country’s domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China’s leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China. That training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren’t serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch. If they can’t provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia’s market share. stories.title: How to Distill Gemini Into an Edge Model
stories.summary: Turn Gemini’s annotations into an edge model for manufacturing inspection. Explore three prompting approaches, review labels, and train RF-DETR model with Roboflow. Deploy the trained model near the camera and keep Gemini available to inspect difficult cases and improve future training data.

sources.name: Roboflow
sources.title: How to Distill Gemini Into an Edge Model
sources.text: To distill Gemini into an edge model, have Gemini label your images, review and correct those labels, then train a small detector that runs next to the camera and does the routine inspections. In Roboflow, auto-label with Gemini through a class description, the Auto Label agent or an Open Prompt Workflow. Then train RF-DETR Small on the reviewed dataset, run it with Inference on your edge device, and route uncertain cases back to Gemini or a human reviewer. Checking an assembly for missing screws takes more than counting detections. A model might miss one screw and mistake a reflection for another, returning the expected count while overlooking an incomplete product. A useful inspection system needs to locate the visible screws at each mounting position and flag images that need further review. With Roboflow, you can use Gemini to help build the training dataset for that system, then train a compact RF-DETR (opens in a new tab) model to detect screws near the camera. In this approach to model distillation , Gemini generates candidate bounding boxes, you review and correct the annotations, and RF-DETR learns the specific detection task. At deployment, the smaller model handles routine detection, while routing logic sends selected difficult images to Gemini or a person for review. In this guide, you’ll explore three ways to prompt Gemini for screw annotations: class descriptions in Roboflow Auto Label, conversational feedback with the Auto Label agent, and an Open Prompt Workflow that returns boxes for inspection in Python. You’ll then review the labels, train RF-DETR Small, test it on your edge hardware, and configure a fallback for uncertain results. Before generating labels, decide exactly what one object means. In our reference image, each screw annotation covers the full visible fastener region, including its outer exposed end and inner metal feature. One screw receives one box. This definition must stay the same across the dataset. Create an Object Detection project and upload the product images (opens in a new tab) . Include complete products, missing screws, reflections, and realistic changes in lighting. In Roboflow Auto Label (opens in a new tab) , the class description is the prompt Gemini uses to find the object . Follow these steps. Gemini searches using that description, and Auto Label saves each resulting annotation as screw . The expected count of four is an application rule. It should not force the teacher to produce four boxes when a screw is missing. You can also describe the labeling task through Chat with Auto Label agent . The agent builds a labeling Workflow from the model and classes and shows a preview. Use the conversation to refine what it should label. The saved annotations still need a class name, which remains screw in this example. See labeling with the Auto Label agent (opens in a new tab) . With Gemini 4 Carbon selected, open Chat with Auto Label agent and enter the following request. Check the preview and request specific corrections. You can use the following correction when that error appears. You can also click an incorrect label or use Flag missing object. Once the preview matches the annotation rule, choose Use this Workflow, confirm the output-class mapping to screw , and select Label batch. Review the job estimate before starting. Continue with the label review in Section 2. This conversation configures the Auto Label Workflow. Gemini 4 Carbon remains the requested annotation model. Check that the saved Workflow uses it. Either setup option produces the same kind of training data for RF-DETR Small. The training examples contain reviewed screw bounding boxes. For this option, you can choose any Gemini model available in the Roboflow Google Gemini block (opens in a new tab) that supports image input and Open Prompt. You can also try different available models with the same prompt and images to compare their bounding boxes. For the Auto Label process above, Roboflow manages the saved annotations. Use the description field or the Auto Label agent conversation above. Neither option requires you to enter a JSON-format prompt or convert coordinates yourself. If you inspect raw Gemini detection output, Google's official object detection documentation (opens in a new tab) specifies box_2d in [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] order, normalized to 0–1000. Normalization expresses a position relative to the image dimensions. A value of 500 is halfway across the relevant dimension, regardless of image size. Use the following conversion for an image of width W and height H. For example, [100, 200, 300, 250] on a 1000-pixel-wide, 600-pixel-high image gives pixel bounds xmin=200, ymin=60, xmax=250, ymax=180. This is a coordinate example, not a measured screw prediction. Prompting Gemini for boxes in a consistent format gives the visualization code a clear schema to check. Gemini models can still format their answers differently even when they receive the same instructions. This Open Prompt test uses a consistent box_2d schema and a model-independent parser. The prompt requests the screw label and [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] coordinates normalized to 0–1000. The script accepts known JSON formatting differences, but checks the coordinates before drawing them. This follows Gemini’s object-detection coordinate convention (opens in a new tab) . The parser uses the requested coordinate order and scale. Numeric checks alone cannot prove that Gemini followed those instructions, so inspect the drawn boxes. Build this small test separately from Auto Label. Use an image input, a text input for the prompt, one Google Gemini block, and two outputs. Follow Build a Workflow (opens in a new tab) . Test with an assembly image and supply the example text in the Workflow’s prompt input. Confirm that both outputs, boxes_json and prompt_echo , appear in the test response. sources.title: Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI model training – here’s how
sources.text: You’ll soon be able to turn off Gemini model training but still retain access to your previous chats with Google’s AI. Google likes to use your conversations with Gemini for model training to help improve the AI. But for people with privacy concerns, the only way to opt out of this was to delete your entire chat history. Now, Google is overhauling the process to eliminate that drawback. Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me In a change set to roll out in the coming weeks, you’ll be able to put the brakes on Gemini model training without losing access to your previous conversations with the AI. Here’s how this works now — and how it will work down the road. Currently, Gemini offers a setting called Keep Activity that controls not only whether and for how long your chats are saved but also whether they’re used to train the AI. You can’t separate the two. To correct this problem, Google will replace Keep Activity with two new settings. With the first setting, you’ll be able to keep or delete your past chats and choose how long your history will be saved. With the second setting, you’ll be able to decide whether your chats, including all text and attachments, will be used for model training. Also: I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes “With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training,” Google said in an announcement shared to Gemini users via email. Here’s how this will play out. If your Keep Activity setting is off when this change is made, both new settings will be off. If your Keep Activity setting is on, both new settings will be on. That means you’ll need to head to Gemini’s Settings if you wish to opt out of model training but still be able to view and access your previous chats. Almost all AIs include a setting for model training that you typically have to manually disable if you’re concerned about your privacy. But most let you opt out without turning off your chat history. ChatGPT offers a setting called “Improve the model for everyone,” which is double-speak for model training. But this is easy enough to turn off. Microsoft Copilot provides settings for “Training on conversation activity” and “Training on voice conversations,” both of which you can disable to opt out of model training. Claude’s AI training option is turned off by default. But you can always control this by checking the setting for “Help improve our AI models.” Also: 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027 (Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.) In all those cases, you still retain access to your conversation history. In contrast, Google has been the only AI player among the majors to impose a restriction for those who want to opt out of AI training. Based on past actions, Google has often earned a reputation for being privacy-unfriendly. I’m glad to see the company take this step in the right direction.
